The old man’s hands were maps of a life spent outdoors, creased and brown like weathered leather. He held the lantern up, and the flame, a timid orange tongue, flickered against the encroaching dusk. Around him, the forest was settling into its nightly chorus—the whisper of leaves, the creak of a distant branch, the low, throaty call of a nightjar. He wasn't lost; he knew every root and stone for miles. He was simply waiting, as he did every autumn evening, for the first firefly of the season. It was a foolish ritual, he knew, a small superstition with no real meaning. But when that single green-gold spark blinked into existence near the mossy trunk of an oak, it felt like a greeting.

The lantern suddenly seemed too bright, too harsh. He snuffed it out with a pinch of his fingers, plunging himself into the soft dark. The firefly pulsed again, closer now, a silent beacon. Then another, and another, until the undergrowth was alive with a constellation of tiny, wandering stars. He smiled, a slow, rare thing that crinkled the corners of his eyes. The world was still full of small miracles, if you knew where to look. He tipped his head back to the sky, where the true stars were just beginning to pierce the velvet blue, and felt, for a moment, perfectly and quietly in his place. The fireflies were his answer. He turned and took the worn path home.
